# Mid-century modern house (Eichler / Palm Springs): FORM PLAN (architect)

Identity: a long, low post-and-beam house in white stucco and dark timber, with a pale near-flat gable roof, deep eaves and beam ends that stick out past them. The street face is blank apart from a tan ledgestone feature wall, a clerestory strip and an orange front door. A flat carport stands to the west with a teal and white car in front of it. The back is all glass, with a kidney pool behind it.
Grid: x 0..33 (west→east, along the street), z 0..33 (z=0 sidewalk on the NORTH street side, z=33 back lot line), y = height.
Ground top = y=0 (bedding y=-1). House floor slab y=1. Walls y=1..5. Roof y=6..7. Chimney to y=8.
Structural rhythm: **beam lines every 3 cells at x = 10,13,16,19,22,25,28,31.** Every post, beam and beam end sits on one of these lines.

## SITE

| mass / feature | x0..x1 | y0..y1 | z0..z1 | notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lot ground (bedding) | 0..33 | -1 | 0..33 | dirt, under everything except the pool |
| Sidewalk | 0..33 | 0 | 0 | smooth_stone, one row along the street |
| Driveway (concrete) | 1..8 | 0 | 1..21 | smooth_stone; joint rows of light_gray_concrete at z=4,8,12,16 |
| Front yard (desert) | 9..33 | 0 | 1..7 | sand; gravel beds at x=22..30 z=1..5 and x=10..16 z=1..5 |
| Stepping-pad path | 18..20 | 0 | 1, 3, 5 | three 3x1 smooth_stone pads in the sand (sand between them) |
| Entry landing | 18..20 | 0 | 6..7 | smooth_stone, under the eave |
| Side strips | 0 (x) / 32..33 | 0 | 1..25 | x=0: sand; x=32..33: sand |
| MAIN HOUSE (shell) | 10..31 | 1..5 | 8..25 | 22 wide x 18 deep; walls on the perimeter |
| Main roof (incl. overhangs) | 9..32 | 6..7 | 6..27 | low gable, ridge along x; see ROOFS |
| Beam ends (exposed tails) | each beam line | 5 | 5 and 28 | 1 cell past the roof edge, front and back |
| ATRIUM (open courtyard, open to the sky) | 17..21 | 1..open | 12..17 | 5x6; glass ring on x=16, x=22, z=11, z=18 |
| Entry recess | 18..20 | 2..4 | 8 | air niche; the door wall sits back at z=9 |
| Stone feature wall | 11..17 | 1..4 | 7 | freestanding 1-thick leaf, 1 proud of the north wall (z=8) |
| CARPORT | 0..9 | 1..5 | 7..21 | flat roof deck y=5 on posts; open N, W; screen at S |
| Carport posts | x=1 | 1..4 | z=8, 14, 20 | dark_oak_log, 1x1 |
| Carport beams | 0..9 | 4 | z=8, 14, 20 | dark_oak_log axis x; the deck sits on them |
| Carport breeze-block screen | 1..9 | 1..4 | 21 | pierced: checkerboard of white_concrete and AIR (holes left open) |
| CAR (reserved, see RESERVED) | 3..5 | 1..2 | 1..7 | parked nose to the street on the driveway, in front of the carport |
| Chimney (fireplace part) | 20..21 | 2..8 | 21..22 | rises through the roof 1 above the ridge band |
| Back patio | 10..31 | 0 | 26..28 | smooth_stone, under/behind the south eave |
| Pool deck | 11..24 | 0 | 29..33 | smooth_stone around the pool |
| KIDNEY POOL (reserved) | 13..22 | -2..0 | 29..32 | see RESERVED for the exact cells |
| Back lawn | 0..10 & 25..33 | 0 | 26..33 | grass_block (x=0..9 z=22..33 included) |
| Palms | (12,3), (30,4), (29,31) | 1..7 | — | jungle trunk + crown, reserved |
| Cactus cluster | 23..29 | 1..3 | 2..4 | on the gravel bed, reserved |
| Mailbox | 9 | 1..2 | 1 | low post + box at the head of the driveway |

## ROOFS

**Main roof: built BY HAND (no preset).** No `$MCD roof` preset fits a mid-century roof: every preset has a pitch of 0.5 or more, and the brief wants a very low gable. The low pitch is the identity, so the roof is a stepped slab gable with the ridge running E-W (along x), its slopes facing the street and the garden. It covers x=9..32 (1 cell of overhang at each gable end) and z=6..27 (2 cells of overhang front and back):

| band | z rows | block / half | y |
|---|---|---|---|
| A, eaves | 6..10 and 23..27 | bottom slab | 6 |
| B | 11..13 and 20..22 | top slab | 6 |
| C | 14..15 and 18..19 | bottom slab | 7 |
| Ridge | 16..17 | top slab | 7 |

- Rise: 1.5 blocks over a 10-cell half-span, the near-flat Eichler gable. The highest point is y=7.
- **Fascia:** the outermost ring (z=6, z=27, x=9, x=32) uses dark_oak_slab at the same half as its band, so a dark line runs round the eave.
- **Atrium hole:** no roof over x=17..21, z=12..17. The edge of the hole is dark_oak_slab, as fascia.
- **Chimney hole:** no roof at x=20..21, z=21..22.
- **Under band C:** the y=6 cells over the interior are air (a raised ceiling vault). The two gable ends close them with glass (see OPENINGS), and so does the atrium ring where it crosses band C (x=16 and x=22, y=6, z=14..17, glass).
- **Beams (exposed):** dark_oak_log with axis z, at y=5 on each beam line x=10,13,...,31, running z=5..28. They pass through the north and south header courses. Inside the house they are ceiling beams with 3 cells of headroom (y=2..4) below them; between the beams the ceiling is at y=5. Outside, they carry the overhang and stick out 1 cell past the fascia at z=5 and z=28. Where the beam on x=19 crosses the atrium it stays as an open beam over the courtyard.
- **Carport roof:** a flat deck, hand built: smooth_stone_slab (bottom half) at y=5 over x=0..9, z=7..21, with a dark_oak_slab fascia on its outer edges (x=0, z=7, z=21). It sits one level below the main roof's west eave (x=9, y=6). The two horizontal planes layered against each other are the mid-century signature.

## FACADES

All walls are white stucco (white_concrete). Every outer wall has the same three layers:

| layer | y | block |
|---|---|---|
| Base (slab edge) | 1 | smooth_stone |
| Body | 2..4 | white stucco, glass or posts |
| Header course | 5 | dark_oak_planks, a continuous dark band under the eave |

The beam ends cross the header.

**North (street, z=8): mostly blank.** From west to east:
- **x=10..17:** blank stucco. In front of it, the **ledgestone feature wall** stands at z=7, x=11..17, y=1..4. It is 1 proud and freestanding, mud_bricks mixed with ~25% packed_mud for the stacked-stone texture. Its top is capped with mud_brick_slab at y=5, but only between the beam lines (x=11,12,14,15,17); the beams at x=13 and x=16 pass over it.
- **x=18..20:** the **entry recess**, 1 deep: the door wall sits at z=9. On it, x=19 is the door, with an orange_concrete transom at y=4. x=18 and x=20 are orange_concrete panels at y=2..4, which makes a bold 3-wide orange door set in white. Reveals at x=17 (stone) and x=21 (stucco).
- **x=21..31:** stucco with the **clerestory strip** in the top course of the body (y=4): glass at x=22..24, 26..27 and 29..30, and dark_oak_log mullions on the beam lines x=25 and x=28. Below it the wall is blank (bedroom wing).
- The 2-cell eave (z=6..7) shades the whole face; the beam ends at z=5 give the rhythm.

**South (garden, z=25): a wall of glass.** The only stucco is the base (y=1) and the header (y=5). Thin dark posts (dark_oak_log, vertical) stand at y=2..4 on every beam line. Between the posts are full-height glass_pane walls (y=2..4), with sliding-door gaps (see OPENINGS). The eave overhangs to z=27 and the beam ends to z=28.

**West (x=10, facing the carport) and East (x=31):** stucco with base and header. Above the header, the gable end shows a glass clerestory band at y=6, z=14..19, between header and roof, and the fascia steps over it. Dark posts at the corners (x=10/31, z=8 and z=25) run y=2..4 on all four corners.

**Atrium ring (inner faces):** glass_pane at y=2..4 (and y=6 where the ring crosses band C), with dark_oak_log posts at the 4 ring corners and on x=19 (z=11, z=18). Header y=5: dark_oak_planks.

Depth summary:

| element | depth relative to the wall plane |
|---|---|
| Feature wall | +1 |
| Beam ends | +3 front and back (past the 2-cell eave) |
| Eaves | +2 front and back, +1 at the gable ends |
| Entry | -1 |
| Glass and posts | flush in the wall plane; the posts read as the wall's structure |

## MATERIALS (all ids checked with `mcd blocks --check`)

| role | block id | why it reads |
|---|---|---|
| Body: stucco walls (~55%) | white_concrete | clean bright white, Palm Springs |
| Structure: posts, beams, beam ends, mullions | dark_oak_log | dark brown, the thin dark posts and exposed beams |
| Header course | dark_oak_planks | a continuous dark band under the eave |
| Fascia | dark_oak_slab | a dark eave line |
| Base course and slab edge | smooth_stone | concrete slab-on-grade |
| Roof deck | smooth_stone_slab | pale grey gravel roof, contrasts with the dark fascia |
| Glass (walls, clerestory, ring) | glass_pane | thin and clear, floor-to-ceiling |
| Feature wall | mud_bricks (+25% packed_mud); cap mud_brick_slab | tan desert ledgestone |
| Front door | acacia_door | reads orange |
| Door surround and transom | orange_concrete | the bold accent (~3%) |
| Breeze-block screen | white_concrete (with air holes) | a pierced white screen |
| Car, lower body | cyan_concrete | saturated teal, not grey |
| Car, roof and top flash | white_concrete | the two-tone |
| Car, bumpers and trim | iron_block | chrome |
| Car, tyres | black_concrete | |
| Car, windows | glass_pane | |
| Driveway, sidewalk, patio, pool deck | smooth_stone | poured concrete |
| Driveway joints | light_gray_concrete | |
| Front yard | sand; gravel beds | desert planting ground |
| Back lawn | grass_block | |
| Bedding | dirt | |
| Pool | water; liner light_blue_concrete; coping smooth_quartz_slab | |
| Palms | jungle_log trunk, jungle_leaves crown | |
| Cacti | cactus | |

Colour scheme: white / dark timber / pale grey roof (the frame), with tan stone, an orange door and a teal car as the accents. The second designer keeps these ids.

## OPENINGS (the shell leaves these as air; doors and panes are added by later parts)

| face | where | size |
|---|---|---|
| North, entry recess | x=18..20, z=8, y=2..4 | air niche 3w x 3h x 1d |
| North, front door | x=19, z=9, y=2..3 | 1w x 2h, acacia_door facing north |
| North, clerestory | z=8, y=4, x=22..24, 26..27, 29..30 | glass strip, 1h |
| West, utility door (kitchen → carport) | x=10, z=10, y=2..3 | 1w x 2h |
| West, dining window | x=10, z=14..16, y=3..4 | 3w x 2h |
| West and East, gable clerestory | x=10 and x=31, y=6, z=14..19 | glass, 6w x 1h |
| East, bedroom 1 window | x=31, z=10..12, y=3..4 | 3w x 2h |
| East, bath clerestory | x=31, z=15..16, y=4 | 2w x 1h |
| East, master bedroom | x=31, z=21..23, y=2..4 | full-height glass |
| South, living slider | x=14..15, z=25, y=2..3 | 2w x 2h opening, glass at y=4 above |
| South, dining/fireplace slider | x=20..21, z=25, y=2..3 | 2w x 2h, glass at y=4 |
| South, master slider | x=26..27, z=25, y=2..3 | 2w x 2h, glass at y=4 |
| Atrium doors | x=19..20, z=11, y=2..3 (from the entry gallery); x=19..20, z=18, y=2..3 (to the living room) | 2w x 2h |

All other bays of the south wall and atrium ring are fixed glass_pane, y=2..4.

## RESERVED (the shell leaves these empty; later parts sink into them or stand on them)

| what | cells |
|---|---|
| Conversation pit | x=13..17, z=20..23, y=1 (no floor slab). The shell lays y=0 there as smooth_quartz, the pit floor; the pit part adds the steps and benches. |
| Freestanding fireplace and chimney | x=20..21, z=21..22, y=1..8 (the floor, beam bays and roof all left open) |
| Atrium planting and paving | x=17..21, z=12..17, y=1 (no slab); y=0 under it is dirt for planting |
| Kidney pool, water y=-1..0, floor y=-2 (ground and bedding left empty) | z=29: x=14..17 and x=20..21 (the pinch at x=18..19 stays deck) |
| | z=30: x=13..22 |
| | z=31: x=13..22 |
| | z=32: x=14..21 |
| Car | x=3..5, y=1..2, z=1..7. Body y=1 over z=1..7, cabin y=2 over z=3..5, wheels at the 4 corners z=2 and z=6. |
| Palms | (12,3), (30,4), (29,31): y=1..7 plus a crown radius of 2 at y=6..7 |
| Cactus bed | x=23..29, z=2..4, y=1..3 |
| Mailbox | (9,1), y=1..2 |
| Patio furniture | x=10..31, z=26..28, y=1 (loungers, by the designer) |

## FLOORS

Single storey. Finished floor y=1, standing height y=2.

| volume | x | z | y (air) | notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Whole house interior | 11..30 | 9..24 | 2..5 | beams at y=5 on the beam lines; extra ceiling void at y=6 for z=14..19 |
| Entry gallery | 17..21 | 9..10 | 2..5 | from the front door to the atrium doors |
| Atrium (outdoor) | 17..21 | 12..17 | open sky | |
| Kitchen (galley + breakfast bar) | 11..15 | 9..13 | 2..5 | utility door to the carport at x=10 |
| Dining | 11..15 | 14..18 | 2..5 | window to the west |
| Living (pit + fireplace) | 11..21 | 19..24 | 2..5 | glass south wall; the pit is reserved as above |
| Bedroom wing corridor | 23..24 | 9..24 | 2..5 | runs along the atrium's east glass |
| Bedroom 1 | 25..30 | 9..13 | 2..5 | |
| Bath 1 and bath 2 | 25..30 | 14..17 | 2..5 | split at x=27/28 |
| Bedroom 2 | 25..30 | 18..20 | 2..5 | small |
| Master bedroom | 23..30 | 21..24 | 2..5 | garden glass and slider |
| West of the atrium | 16 | 12..17 | — | the atrium ring; the kitchen and dining open onto it through the glass |
| Carport (outdoor) | 1..9 | 7..20 | 1..4 | under the deck at y=5 |

Interior partitions sit only between the beam lines or on them, and never reach above y=5.

name: minecraft-design
description: Design-first Minecraft building — concept builds, making plain functional builds (redstone rooms, procedural houses, corridors, roads) look like a skilled human built them, designed type programs for generators, and rendering/checking structure .nbt files without the game. Use whenever a Minecraft build "works but looks bad", when asked to design, decorate, beautify, style, render or review a Minecraft build, or when an agent focused on redstone/layout/procedural generation should hand decor to a specialist.

# Minecraft design

You design Minecraft builds the way a skilled human builder does, and you can see them: the toolkit renders
structure `.nbt` files headlessly with the game's real block models, so **every design decision gets checked by
looking**. This doctrine comes from a long measured study (concept→doc→build→revise pipelines, a facade
benchmark, a failed mesh-to-voxel detour, and decor work on a real procedural redstone town). Follow it.

Toolkit: `node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/tools/bin/mcd.mjs <command>` (Node 20+, nothing to install; it fetches the
Minecraft client jar from Mojang once and caches it). Details: [references/toolkit.md](references/toolkit.md).

## The five rules that decide the look

1. **Design first; decorate never.** The ugliest results come from decoration applied to a form someone else
   (an algorithm, a redstone layout) already fixed: trim on a box is still a box. The best results come from
   deciding the *form* — massing, roof, openings, depth — as a designer. If you are asked to "decorate" a plain
   build, you are allowed (expected) to change its form wherever function and the user's constraints allow.
2. **Function is a contract, not an afterthought.** Whatever must keep working (redstone, rails, doors, walk
   paths, reserved machine space, street clearances) is written down as hard constraints *before* designing,
   and checked by code after (`mcd check before after`). A design pass that respects a written contract stays
   bold without breaking anything; one that guesses either breaks function or gets timid. See
   [references/function-contract.md](references/function-contract.md).
3. **Name the blocker; don't settle.** When the look you need is blocked by a contract term (a visible
   placeholder block, a no-projection rule, a reserved volume), say exactly which term and what it costs, so the
   owner can trade it. Quietly delivering half the design is the failure mode.
4. **Author as code, one bay at a time.** Write a short generator script (`mcd new`) using the build library:
   design one bay as a function, tile it on the rhythm, mirror for symmetry. Typing coordinates is where time
   and errors go; code makes cost scale with design decisions, not block count. **Curves and massing come from
   shape brushes**, never hand-placed blocks: `dome`, `cylinder`, `minaret`, `arch`
   ([references/shapes-curved.md](references/shapes-curved.md)); `setbacks`, `gableRoof`, `hipRoof`, `fins`,
   `parapet`, `cornice`, `falseFront`, `stepGable` ([references/shapes-massing.md](references/shapes-massing.md)).
   Hand-placed domes and setbacks came out faceted, too small, or as a flat box with a decorated front.
   **Roofs come from `mcd roof` / `roof()` by style name** (gable, hip, pyramid, mansard, gambrel, flat-parapet,
   shed, dutch-gable; with eaves, cornice, dormers, pediment, crest, chimneys, a tower): [references/roofs.md](references/roofs.md).
   **The site is part of the design**: terrain, sedimentary ledges, boulders, streams and waterfalls, woods, paths
   and bridges come from the landscaping brushes ([references/landscaping.md](references/landscaping.md)), checked
   with `mcd check --site`.
5. **Judge from where a person stands, and keep the better.** Render after every pass and *look* (Read the
   PNGs). Judge streets from eye height, interiors from inside (`--eye/--look`), never only from a flat
   elevation. A second pass is a coin flip unless you compare it to the first and keep the better one.

## Modes — pick one from context

| Mode | When | Output |
|---|---|---|
| **Concept** (`/minecraft-design:concept`) | "design a bakery / a canal row / a workshop" — nothing exists yet | `.nbt` + sheet |
| **Beautify an instance** (`/minecraft-design:beautify`) | a specific plain build exists (`.nbt`): an operator room, a hallway, a house | new `.nbt` (never overwrite) + before/after sheet + check report |
| **Type program** (`/minecraft-design:program`) | buildings come from a generator (procedural town, street of templates) — hand-editing one instance gets overwritten | a parametric generator module + contract + sheets on several instances |
| **Review** (`/minecraft-design:render`, `/minecraft-design:check`) | look at or audit any build | sheets, check report |
| **Build** (`/minecraft-design:build`, experimental) | good-at-a-glance builds from a one-line brief, unattended | `.nbt` + card, every version kept; revise with a comment ([references/build-workflow.md](references/build-workflow.md)) |

Generator work is the trap: in a procedural town the only edit that holds is a change to the *type*, and the
best one is a designed type program the generator places — not trim knobs on its massing (measured: trim on
fixed massing barely registers; a design-first type reads as a real building).

## The design procedure (all modes)

1. **Read** the build and its context. `mcd info`, `mcd check`, `mcd render` — look at the sheet. What is it
   for, where does it sit (biome, neighbours, base materials, era), who uses it, what must keep working?
2. **Write the contract** (function, envelope, clearances, footprint) — from the build, the user, or the host
   project's rules. Unknown host rules are worth one look in the host repo before designing.
3. **Write a design brief** (≤200 words, in your reasoning or `brief.md`):
   - **Identity** in one line, from context — *never default to generic medieval cobble-and-oak*.
   - **Palette by role**: dominant ~60%, supporting ~30%, accent ~10%, 3–6 blocks, a named relationship
     ("dark timber / ochre render / grey stone"), each with a diegetic reason (what this place is built of).
     Colour needs a reason, not permission. Check contrast — trim that doesn't contrast doesn't read.
   - **Massing & roof**: the volumes and roof forms, their edges (verges, eaves, ridges).
   - **Rhythm**: bay width and what repeats in each bay.
   - **Base / middle / top**: plinth / body / cornice-roofline outside; floor / walls / ceiling inside.
   - **Depth plan**: what stands proud (+1/+2) and what recesses (−1/−2).
   - Optional: `mcd concept` for concept art when `GEMINI_API_KEY` is set — a strong craft reference.
4. **Build as code** (`mcd new build.mjs [--from in.nbt]`), in fenced passes, rendering after each:
   1. *Form*: massing, roof, openings — the part decoration can never fix later. Use the shape brushes; check
      the silhouette in the 3/4 view against the concept before any detail.
   2. *Structure & depth*: frames, posts, beams, piers proud of the wall; panels and openings recessed.
   3. *Materials* by role.
   4. *Detail*: sub-block pieces carry the craft (see [references/craft.md](references/craft.md)). Detail is its own
      phase, after the form is final, and can go to a cheap subagent: rules on face maps (`mcd faces`, `mcd paint`,
      [references/detail-language.md](references/detail-language.md)) or operations on named features
      (`mcd features`, `mcd detail`, [references/detailing.md](references/detailing.md)). Keep the undetailed build
      if the detail reads busier rather than better (texture mixes are the usual culprit). Ready-made craft brushes
      (plaque, signboard, bunting, profiled pilasters, surrounds, glazing, weather/vary presets, fixtures, planters,
      railing, finial, louvres, brackets) and roof PRESETS (`mcd roof --preset cottage|shop|townhouse|civic|temple|
      granary|modern`) beat hand-placed blocks: see references/craft.md for when to use which.
   5. *Inspect before you finish*: `mcd check` (floating, unsupported, orphan blocks), `mcd palette` (roof/trim
      contrast, outlier materials), `mcd render --closeups` (entrance, eaves, small features at readable size), and
      `mcd diff before after --fail-empty` after any change (a change nobody can see is not a change).
   5. *Light & life*: lights on the rhythm, a few props that say who uses it.
5. **Check and compare.** `mcd check before after` must be OK (0 violations). `mcd compare` for a before/after
   sheet. Fix the largest remaining blank surface (the check lists them). Revert a pass that made it worse.
6. **Report** (≤10 lines): identity, palette, what changed, contract result, any blocker terms named, files.

## Calibration (what we measured)

- Raise the bar, never cap: models under-detail to whatever bar they infer. Ask for showcase depth.
- One pass can't push every dimension; a "more detail" push drowned colour. Fence the passes.
- First drafts over-decorate (bands on every floor read as stripes; every-other-course quoins read as a
  checkerboard). Restraint — one strong line, paired quoins, rest areas — wins on the glance.
- Relief is construction, not recolour: swapping a wall's block is not detail; things standing proud are.
- Recess by exclusion: there is no "air op" in your head — carve a niche by *not placing* the wall block, and
  remember a recess in a 1-thick wall opens to whatever is behind it (back it).
- A rule that fails first: before trusting a protection, break it on purpose and watch the check catch it.
- Don't trust self-reported effort or time; measure. Don't trust a single numeric judge; compare pairwise.

## Model choice (measured, 2026-10-08)

**Sonnet 5.5 is the default** (the `decorator` subagent runs on it): near-Opus builds at about ⅓ the cost.
Use **Opus 5.5** for final passes and long reference-heavy builds; **Haiku 5.5** (default effort) for cheap drafts and
reviews, since it under-builds on long tasks. **Max effort** helps only in iterative, tool-using passes, never in a
single long generation (there it burned 535k tokens for a worse result).

Pitfalls with evidence: [references/pitfalls.md](references/pitfalls.md). Domain playbooks (shopfronts, rows,
corridors, operator rooms, roads, bridges): [references/playbooks.md](references/playbooks.md).

**Big builds span sessions.** Each session works to a clock (`--minutes`: 45 for a build, 15 for a revise). The first
build session saves a whole first pass (massing and shell) by a third of the way in; every later save is a whole
building. With more than one session allowed, the first writes `plan.md` before building (every mass with block
coordinates, palette by role, one shared vocabulary of windows, caps and cornices, one generator module per part, a
checklist in order); every later session follows it and ticks it off, so the parts cohere. A session that can't finish answers `finished: false` with what is left, and the next session (up to
`--sessions`, default 2) continues from the files in the run dir: the generator scripts, `build.nbt`, `elements.md`,
and the transcripts. A fresh session also means a fresh context window, so size isn't capped by one session's memory.
`summary.json` says `finished` and how many `sessions` were used.

**Lean mode (`--lean`) is the minimal-spend setting.** One Sonnet session DESIGNS and writes no code (its output is
the scarce spend): `elements.md` (the required elements, each with its real construction) and `plan.md` (every mass
with block coordinates, the palette by role, the vocabulary of repeated elements and furniture, the interior, every
opening, the parts with their specs). Two Haiku sessions then write the kit from it, at once: the vocabulary
(`palette.json` with ids checked, `vocab.mjs` with a tested helper per vocabulary item) and the scaffold (one stub
module per part, `build.mjs`, and `make.sh`, the one command that builds `build.nbt`, roof preset included). Then one Codex conversation (`tools/bin/codex-shim.mjs`, a BAML client on the
ChatGPT plan) draws concept art of the planned site from the planner's description and palette, and in the same turn
reports the prompt it used and the block palette it drew with (`concept.json`). That palette, with ids checked against
the game, becomes `palette.json`, so the workers build from the ids the picture was made of instead of guessing. A
`--concept` the user gave is used instead; without Codex there's no art and the planner's palette stands. `build.mjs` runs the parts through `runParts`: a later part can only add into
air (it can't break an earlier part's wall), and every off-palette block is reported; the art's palette adds to the
planner's, never shrinks it. After each part the workflow rebuilds and reads `parts-report.json`: a part that left
refused writes or off-palette blocks gets one short Haiku session to fix exactly those. Then the parts are built by short Haiku sessions (at most `--sessions` parts, default 6, of `--minutes`,
default 12), each filling in only its own module, running `make.sh`, checking, rendering and ticking the plan: the
first part (massing and shell) alone, then every other part AT ONCE, each in its own copy of the run (`crew/`), the whole
wave at once (`--crew`, default 24). The modules are merged back and rebuilt in plan order; parts that clash in the merge get parallel fix
sessions. Every room in the plan gets its own Haiku INTERIOR DESIGNER in that parallel wave (purpose, mood and key pieces
from the plan; the layout and furniture are theirs, kept walkable). Last, a Haiku INSPECTOR runs `mcd walk` (can a
player walk from the entrance into every room?) and renders the whole, fixing what fell between the parts.
Planning is split by default: `--form-planner` (default opus@medium; `none` for one planner) is the architect and
decides the form in plan.md (site, masses, roofs, facades, the colour scheme's block ids, openings, reserved cells,
floors), and `--planner` (default sonnet@medium), the designer, adds the elements, palette, vocabulary, rooms and parts inside it; any model may carry an effort, e.g. `haiku@medium`
(the kit writer runs at medium: most of Haiku's output at high effort is thinking). The planner holds the design, the workers hold the labour. A lean revise is
Haiku, 10 minutes x 2. Models are the aliases (`haiku`, `sonnet`): always the latest. Rerunning a stopped lean build keeps its `plan.json` and `concept.png` instead of paying for
them again. **Plan once, build many:** after planning and art, the run keeps them pristine in `plan-kit/`, and
`build --from-plan <that run> --dir <new run>` starts another Haiku crew from it with no planner or art cost (for
variants to pick from, or a retry). `--model <id>` picks any other builder model.

**Nothing is lost if a session overruns.** The hard limit is 15 minutes past the clock. A session cut off there keeps
its last `build.nbt`, the next session is told it was cut off and where its transcript is, `sessions/*.jsonl` holds
every session's full transcript, and the ledger gets a row with its tokens (`cost: null`, `stopped`). A watchdog stops
the `claude` process when the workflow gives up, so nothing keeps running and spending unseen.

floors), and `--planner` (default sonnet@medium), the designer, adds the elements, palette, vocabulary, rooms and parts inside it; any model may carry an effort, e.g. `haiku@medium`
(the kit writer runs at medium: most of Haiku's output at high effort is thinking). The planner holds the design, the workers hold the labour. A lean revise is
Haiku, 10 minutes x 2. Models are the aliases (`haiku`, `sonnet`): always the latest. Rerunning a stopped lean build keeps its `plan.json` and `concept.png` instead of paying for
them again. **Plan once, build many:** after planning and art, the run keeps them pristine in `plan-kit/`, and
`build --from-plan <that run> --dir <new run>` starts another Haiku crew from it with no planner or art cost (for
variants to pick from, or a retry). `--model <id>` picks any other builder model.

**Nothing is lost if a session overruns.** The hard limit is 15 minutes past the clock. A session cut off there keeps
its last `build.nbt`, the next session is told it was cut off and where its transcript is, `sessions/*.jsonl` holds
every session's full transcript, and the ledger gets a row with its tokens (`cost: null`, `stopped`). A watchdog stops
the `claude` process when the workflow gives up, so nothing keeps running and spending unseen.

input.concept_subject: A single-storey 1950s-60s California Eichler/Palm Springs house on a flat suburban lot, seen from the street corner: a long, low white-stucco block under a pale grey near-flat gable roof (stepped slabs, ridge running along the street) with deep eaves edged in a dark timber fascia and dark log beam ends sticking out past the eaves every three blocks. The street face is almost blank white with a dark band under the eave, a strip of clerestory glass with dark mullions near the roofline on the east half, a freestanding tan ledgestone feature wall on the west half, and a recessed entry with a bold orange door and orange panels, reached by three stepping pads across a sand and gravel desert front yard with cacti (a tall saguaro and barrel cacti) and two palms and a low mailbox at the driveway head. To the west a flat carport on thin dark posts, its roof deck one level below the main eave, a pierced white breeze-block screen at its back, and in front of it on a light concrete driveway with joint lines a teal-and-white finned 1950s car nose to the street. The garden side behind is floor-to-ceiling glass between thin dark posts with sliding-door gaps, opening to a smooth concrete patio with white loungers and a kidney-shaped turquoise pool with white coping, lawn and a third palm. In the middle of the house an open-sky atrium courtyard in a glass ring with ferns and a small tree; the clerestory gable ends are glazed.

structured_output.concept_subject: A single-storey 1950s-60s California Eichler/Palm Springs house on a flat suburban lot, seen from the street corner: a long, low white-stucco block under a pale grey near-flat gable roof (stepped slabs, ridge running along the street) with deep eaves edged in a dark timber fascia and dark log beam ends sticking out past the eaves every three blocks. The street face is almost blank white with a dark band under the eave, a strip of clerestory glass with dark mullions near the roofline on the east half, a freestanding tan ledgestone feature wall on the west half, and a recessed entry with a bold orange door and orange panels, reached by three stepping pads across a sand and gravel desert front yard with cacti (a tall saguaro and barrel cacti) and two palms and a low mailbox at the driveway head. To the west a flat carport on thin dark posts, its roof deck one level below the main eave, a pierced white breeze-block screen at its back, and in front of it on a light concrete driveway with joint lines a teal-and-white finned 1950s car nose to the street. The garden side behind is floor-to-ceiling glass between thin dark posts with sliding-door gaps, opening to a smooth concrete patio with white loungers and a kidney-shaped turquoise pool with white coping, lawn and a third palm. In the middle of the house an open-sky atrium courtyard in a glass ring with ferns and a small tree; the clerestory gable ends are glazed.
